title: Exploring the Gapminder Dataset with R
text:
Introduction
In this post, I will explore the Gapminder dataset using R. The goal is to look at differences in life expectancy and GDP per capita across continents, and then look at how life expectancy has changed over time for one country.
The data comes from the Gapminder dataset and is available in R through the gapminder package.


Load the packages

library(gapminder)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

The gapminder dataset contains information about countries across several years, including population, life expectancy, and GDP per capita.


Look at the most recent year
For the first part of the analysis, I will focus on the year 2007 and select only the variables that are useful for this comparison.

gapminder_2007 <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  select(country, continent, lifeExp, gdpPercap, pop)

head(gapminder_2007)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  country     continent lifeExp gdpPercap      pop
  <fct>       <fct>       <dbl>     <dbl>    <int>
1 Afghanistan Asia         43.8      975. 31889923
2 Albania     Europe       76.4     5937.  3600523
3 Algeria     Africa       72.3     6223. 33333216
4 Angola      Africa       42.7     4797. 12420476
5 Argentina   Americas     75.3    12779. 40301927
6 Australia   Oceania      81.2    34435. 20434176


The resulting dataset contains one observation for each country in 2007.


Average life expectancy by continent
Next, I will group the countries by continent and calculate the average life expectancy for each continent.

continent_summary <- gapminder_2007 |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(
    average_life_expectancy = mean(lifeExp),
    average_gdp_per_capita = mean(gdpPercap)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(average_life_expectancy))

continent_summary

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  continent average_life_expectancy average_gdp_per_capita
  <fct>                       <dbl>                  <dbl>
1 Oceania                      80.7                 29810.
2 Europe                       77.6                 25054.
3 Americas                     73.6                 11003.
4 Asia                         70.7                 12473.
5 Africa                       54.8                  3089.


This table allows us to compare the average life expectancy and GDP per capita across continents. The continents with higher average GDP per capita also tend to have higher average life expectancy in this dataset.


GDP per capita and life expectancy
We can also look at the relationship between GDP per capita and life expectancy for individual countries in 2007.

ggplot(
  data = gapminder_2007,
  mapping = aes(
    x = gdpPercap,
    y = lifeExp,
    colour = continent
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "GDP per Capita",
    y = "Life Expectancy",
    colour = "Continent"
  ) +
  theme_bw()







Figure 1: GDP per capita and life expectancy for countries in 2007.





The scatter plot shows that countries with higher GDP per capita generally have higher life expectancy. There are also noticeable differences between continents.


Life expectancy in Canada over time
Finally, I will look at how life expectancy changed over time in Canada.

canada_data <- gapminder |>
  filter(country == "Canada")

canada_data

# A tibble: 12 × 6
   country continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
   <fct>   <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
 1 Canada  Americas   1952    68.8 14785584    11367.
 2 Canada  Americas   1957    70.0 17010154    12490.
 3 Canada  Americas   1962    71.3 18985849    13462.
 4 Canada  Americas   1967    72.1 20819767    16077.
 5 Canada  Americas   1972    72.9 22284500    18971.
 6 Canada  Americas   1977    74.2 23796400    22091.
 7 Canada  Americas   1982    75.8 25201900    22899.
 8 Canada  Americas   1987    76.9 26549700    26627.
 9 Canada  Americas   1992    78.0 28523502    26343.
10 Canada  Americas   1997    78.6 30305843    28955.
11 Canada  Americas   2002    79.8 31902268    33329.
12 Canada  Americas   2007    80.7 33390141    36319.


The filtered dataset contains the observations for Canada from 1952 to 2007.

ggplot(
  data = canada_data,
  mapping = aes(
    x = year,
    y = lifeExp
  )
) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Life Expectancy"
  ) +
  theme_bw()







Figure 2: Life expectancy in Canada from 1952 to 2007.





The graph shows that life expectancy in Canada increased steadily over the period represented in the Gapminder dataset.


Conclusion
This analysis used the Gapminder dataset to explore life expectancy and GDP per capita. The 2007 data shows differences between continents and suggests a positive relationship between GDP per capita and life expectancy. Looking at Canada separately also shows that life expectancy increased over time.

Introduction
In this post, we will explore the Palmer Penguins dataset using Python. We will compare the body mass and flipper length of the three penguin species and create a small summary of the data.
The data comes from the Palmer Penguins dataset, collected by Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. The dataset is available directly through the palmerpenguins Python package.

The dataset contains measurements for Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins. The columns contain information such as species, island, bill measurements, flipper length, body mass, and sex.


Clean the data

penguins_clean = penguins[
    [
        "species",
        "island",
        "bill_length_mm",
        "flipper_length_mm",
        "body_mass_g"
    ]
].dropna()

print("Cleaned Penguin dataset with ",penguins_clean.shape[0]," rows and ",penguins_clean.shape[1]," columns:")

Here we have selected the variables that we want to analyse, while removing the observations with missing values. This makes the summary calculations in the next step much easier to interpret.


Compare the species

species_summary = (
    penguins_clean
    .groupby("species")
    .agg(
        number_of_penguins = ("species", "size"),
        average_body_mass_g = ("body_mass_g", "mean"),
        average_flipper_length_mm = ("flipper_length_mm", "mean")
    )
    .round(1)
)

species_summary.sort_values(by=["average_body_mass_g","average_flipper_length_mm"],ascending = False)

The summary table shows clear differences between the three penguin species. In particular, Gentoo penguins tend to have a larger average body mass and longer flippers than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.


Find the species with the highest average body mass

heaviest_species = species_summary["average_body_mass_g"].idxmax()

print("Species with the highest average body mass:", heaviest_species)

Species with the highest average body mass: Gentoo


This confirms from the calculated summary that Gentoo penguins have the highest average body mass in this dataset.


Conclusion
This small analysis demonstrates that the three penguin species differ in their physical measurements. Gentoo penguins stand out because they are, on average, heavier and have longer flippers than the other two species.

title: About
text:
I am a mechanical engineering graduate from India, and before joining the Master of Data Science (MDS) program at UBC, I worked as a software developer at Dassault Systèmes for over three years. Although my academic background is in mechanical engineering, my professional experience gradually shifted my interests toward software development, algorithms, and eventually data science.
At Dassault Systèmes, I worked primarily with C++ on CATIA, an engineering software platform used for designing and developing complex products. My work involved developing and improving algorithms for engineering applications, particularly for electrical systems. I often worked on problems where there was no straightforward solution, which required understanding the engineering problem, breaking it down into smaller components, and designing algorithmic approaches and heuristics to solve it.
This experience helped me develop strong problem-solving and programming skills and also showed me how software and computational methods can be used to solve real-world engineering problems. Over time, I became increasingly interested in how data-driven methods, machine learning, and statistical techniques could complement traditional algorithmic approaches and help solve problems that are difficult to address using explicitly defined rules alone.
This interest motivated me to explore data science independently through courses and personal projects involving Python, machine learning, and deep learning. Through these experiences, I realized that I wanted a stronger and more structured foundation in areas such as statistics, machine learning, data analysis, and data visualization.
I therefore joined the Master of Data Science program at UBC to build on my existing engineering and software development experience while developing these new skills. My goal is to learn how to approach real-world problems from a data-driven perspective and eventually combine my background in engineering, software development, and data science to build practical and meaningful solutions.
